course.title: Next Token
course.subtitle: Large language models, set by hand
course.description: An interactive course on large language models from the inside out: how a model picks the next token, how to build reliable things with it, how models are trained, and how to ship AI features without getting burned. Set in a letterpress print shop.

shell.resetBody: Every sort goes back to its case: progress, predictions and settings on this device. The downloaded model stays in your browser's cache.
shell.honor: Nothing here does the exercise for you. You predict first; the bench checks after.

bench.copyHint: Type a few words. The compositor breaks them into sorts.
bench.proofEmpty: Nothing set yet. The paper waits.
bench.space: A leading dot is a space. It belongs to the sort.
bench.byteFragment: Part of a character. It takes more than one sort to print it.

tokenizers.o200kNote: OpenAI's tokenizer for the GPT-4o family, via js-tiktoken
tokenizers.qwenNote: the tokenizer of the model on this bench
tokenizers.claudeNote: Claude uses its own tokenizer. Exact Claude counts come only from Anthropic's token-counting API, so they are not shown here.

model.title: The compositor is not on the bench yet
model.body: Live fans need a small model running in your browser. Nothing leaves your device. It downloads once and stays in your browser's cache.
model.englishOnly: Mostly English. Spanish fans will look strange, and that is a lesson too.
model.thinking: The compositor is reading the line…
model.recorded: Recorded run · {model} · {date}. Models change; so do results.
model.noRecording: No recording for this line. Load the compositor to set your own words.

fan.label: The fan: what could come next

remark.greedy: Zero. The compositor takes the likeliest sort every time. Same copy, same line.
remark.cold: Cold. The compositor reaches for the same sort almost every time.
remark.warm: Warm. Usually the likely sort; now and then the second.
remark.hot: Hot. Unlikely sorts get a real chance. So do mistakes.
remark.scalding: Scalding. The case is wide open and the compositor is guessing.

fan.pickHint: Or pick a sort by hand.
fan.pulled: Outside top-p: the compositor won't touch it

problem.heading: The bill went up in Spanish.
problem.body: Mercadito translated its help assistant for customers in Mexico. Same answers, same traffic, same model. The invoice for the Spanish assistant came in higher anyway. Nobody changed a setting. Something about the words themselves costs more.
problem.task: Find out what the model is actually charged for.

bench.heading: Set some copy.
bench.body: The model never sees letters or words. It sees sorts: pieces of text from a fixed case, each with a number. Type anything and watch two different cases break it up.
bench.observe: Look for: words that take one sort, words that take several, and how spaces travel with the sort after them.

measure.heading: Same message, two languages.
measure.body: Here is one of Mercadito's real-shaped replies, in English and in Spanish. Predict first, then set both.
measure.predict: Which version will take more sorts?
measure.ratio: Spanish takes {ratio}× the sorts of English on {tokenizer}.

cost.heading: What that does to the bill
cost.priceNote: An example rate. Put in your provider's current price; they change.
cost.perConversation: Sorts per conversation are scaled from the sample.
cost.difference: Same conversations, {difference} more a month in Spanish.

debrief.heading: The case was cut for English.

points.one: Models read and bill by token, not by word or character. A token is whatever the tokenizer's fixed vocabulary says it is.
points.two: Tokenizers learn their vocabulary from training text. When most of that text is English, common English words get a sort of their own and Spanish words get split.
points.three: Different models use different cases. The same copy has a different count, and a different price, on each.
points.four: Count with the tokenizer of the model you will pay for. For Claude, that means the token-counting API.

debrief.voice: The compositor doesn't read words. It reads whatever the case was cut to hold.

problem.heading: Forty mugs, one description.
problem.body: Mercadito's product-copy writer produced descriptions for forty different mugs. All forty came back word for word identical. The prompt was fine. Someone had set the temperature to zero.
problem.task: See what temperature actually changes, with a real model.

bench.heading: Open the fan.
bench.body: At every step the compositor scores every sort in the case. The fan shows the likeliest ones, each set at a size that matches its probability. Move the temperature and watch the fan open and close.
bench.observe: Pick a sort by hand, or let the compositor draw. Then set the next one.
bench.pieces: Some sorts are pieces of words. The compositor builds a word one sort at a time, and in Spanish that happens more often.

measure.heading: Twenty draws.
measure.body: From the same line, the compositor draws twenty times at a cold setting and twenty times at a hot one. Predict first.
measure.seed: Draws are seeded, so this run repeats exactly.

debrief.heading: Temperature reshapes; it doesn't know more.

points.one: The model produces one score (a logit) for every sort in its case. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities.
points.two: Temperature divides the scores before softmax. Low values sharpen the fan toward the top sort; high values flatten it.
points.three: Top-p keeps the smallest set of sorts whose probabilities add up to p, and drops the long tail.
points.four: The likeliest sort is not the true one. The compositor knows what usually comes next, not what is correct.

debrief.voice: Fluent is not the same as correct.

problem.heading: The refund nobody approved.
problem.body: A long chat with Mercadito's support assistant ended in an automatic refund of $2,450. The system prompt says refunds over $2,000 need a supervisor. The model had followed that rule all week. On this chat it didn't.
problem.task: Find out where the rule went.

bench.heading: Fill the stick.
bench.body: The model reads everything it is given, system message included, from one composing stick of fixed length. Set the conversation one message at a time and watch what happens when the stick is full.
bench.observe: Change the shop rule for a full stick and set the conversation again.

measure.heading: Where things get lost.
measure.body: Even what stays on the stick isn't read equally well everywhere. Predict first, then look at a real measurement.

debrief.heading: What doesn't fit, doesn't exist.

points.one: A model's context window is a fixed number of tokens. System prompt, conversation, documents and the reply all share it.
points.two: When it fills, something has to go. Which thing is a product decision your code makes, not the model.
points.three: Pin what must never fall off (rules, identity), and summarize what can be shortened. Summaries lose detail too.
points.four: Staying in the window is not the same as being used: position matters, and how much depends on the model. Measure yours.

debrief.voice: The stick is full. Something falls off the end.

problem.heading: Three studies, one real.
problem.body: Mercadito's marketing team drafted a blog post about why the Spanish assistant costs more. It cites three studies. Legal wants to know if they exist before it goes out.
problem.task: Watch where citations like these come from, then check them.

bench.heading: Let it write references.
bench.body: The compositor is given the start of a reference list with one real paper. It continues the list the way reference lists usually continue.
bench.observe: Mark each reference before you check it.

measure.heading: Check the catalog.
measure.body: Each reference is looked up by title. Compare what you marked with what the catalog says, and how confident the compositor was.

debrief.heading: The compositor doesn't know what's true.

points.one: A language model produces likely text. A plausible reference and a real reference look the same to it.
points.two: Confidence (high probability) measures fluency, not truth. Invented titles can be set with dark ink.
points.three: Instruction tuning and newer training can teach models to hedge or decline, as the larger model did. It reduces fabrication; it doesn't remove it.
points.four: Never trust a citation, number or quote from a model without checking it against a source. Make the check part of the product.

debrief.voice: The compositor doesn't know what's true. It knows what usually comes next.

problem.heading: The refunds bot that wrote essays.
problem.body: Mercadito's returns desk wanted a bot that answers one question: is this return eligible? Its output feeds an automation that only understands yes or no. Marketing rewrote the prompt to sound warmer. The automation started failing.
problem.task: Compare the two prompts on the same cases and let an eval decide.

bench.heading: Two job tickets.
bench.body: Same policy, same cases. Prompt A states what the output must be. Prompt B reads better. Look at both before you predict.
bench.observe: With a live model in Outside work you can edit either prompt; recorded runs only cover these exact words.

measure.heading: The duel.
measure.body: Ten customer messages, both prompts. One grader checks the reply is exactly one word; a second model reads each reply and checks the verdict is right.

debrief.heading: A prompt is a specification.

points.one: Write the prompt for whoever consumes the output: a person, a parser, or another program. Say what the output must look like.
points.two: Warmth and length are not quality. Measure the thing the product needs, on cases, not on one example you liked.
points.three: Even a precise prompt gets cases wrong. The eval found them; reading two good answers would not have.
points.four: Keep the cases. Every prompt change from now on runs against them before it ships.

debrief.voice: Lovely prompt. Your eval says it's worse.

problem.heading: Forty mugs, revisited.
problem.body: After the temperature fix, Mercadito's product copy got prettier. Then a customer returned a mug described as dishwasher safe. The spec sheet said hand wash only.
problem.task: Build an eval that would have caught it, and find out what an LLM judge catches and misses.

bench.heading: Choose your cases and your graders.
bench.body: Pick the spec sheets to test and the graders to apply. Cheap exact checks catch some failures; a judge model reads for meaning but has its own taste.
bench.observe: An eval with no cases is a guess. Pick at least three.

measure.heading: Run your eval.
measure.body: Two prompts write descriptions for your cases. Predict which scores higher, then read where your graders and the judge agree and where they don't.

debrief.heading: Graders have blind spots; so do judges.

points.one: Start with exact, cheap checks for what must never happen: invented claims, missing facts, wrong format.
points.two: An LLM judge reads meaning, but it applies its own standards and drifts from your rubric. Check it against cases you graded yourself.
points.three: A judge can catch what your rules missed and fail what your rules allow. Both are information about your eval, not truth.
points.four: Grow the eval from real failures. Every complaint is a case.

debrief.voice: No test cases. You are guessing.

problem.heading: The press jammed on a fence.
problem.body: Mercadito's returns desk turned customer emails into job sheets with a model. The prompt said 'reply with a JSON object'. Most mornings the importer stopped on the first sheet: the JSON came wrapped in a Markdown fence.
problem.task: See how often that happens, what a retry costs, and what a schema changes.

bench.heading: The press accepts only what fits.
bench.body: The press is the validator: a sheet must parse as JSON and match the schema, field by field. Feed the same six emails asked nicely, then constrained by the schema.
bench.observe: Read why each rejected sheet was rejected, and what the retry sent back.

measure.heading: Count the jams.
measure.body: Predict first, then run both modes and compare first-try acceptance, retries, wrong fields and the extra calls.

debrief.heading: Validate every sheet. Constrain when you can.

points.one: A prompt that describes a format is a request, not a guarantee. Parse and validate every response before you use it.
points.two: Send structured outputs (a JSON Schema) when your provider supports them: the model can only emit text that fits.
points.three: A retry with the validator's reason usually fixes a rejected sheet, at the price of another call, more tokens and more latency.
points.four: Valid is not right. A sheet can match the schema and still carry the wrong reason or the wrong order number; that is what evals are for.

debrief.voice: The press rejects a malformed sheet. It can't tell you the sheet is wrong.

problem.heading: The assistant refunded a blender. Who pressed the button?
problem.body: Mercadito's support assistant now has two tools: look up an order and issue a refund. The first week, a 2,450 MXN refund went out for a cracked jar. Finance asked which part of the system decided to pay.
problem.task: Run the conversation as the executor and see what the model actually controls.

bench.heading: The model asks. You run.
bench.body: Each turn the model either asks for a tool or replies. Every request lands on your desk first: you choose what the lookup returns, and whether the refund runs.
bench.observe: Try a wrong row, a missing order and a refused refund. Read what the model does with each.

measure.heading: Hand it the wrong row.
measure.body: Predict first, then hand back the coffee order on the first lookup and read the model's next move.

debrief.heading: The model writes requests. Your code holds the keys.

points.one: A tool call is text: a name and arguments. Nothing runs until your code runs it, so every permission check belongs in your code, not in the prompt.
points.two: The model treats tool results as facts. Wrong data from your tool becomes the model's answer, unless something in the loop checks it.
points.three: Refuse dangerous calls in code and hand the reason back as the result; the model can then explain it to the customer.
points.four: Cap the loop. A harness stops after a fixed number of steps, whatever the model asks for next.

debrief.voice: The press doesn't pick the paper. Whoever feeds it does.

problem.heading: The handbook said 15 days. The assistant said 30.
problem.body: Mercadito's assistant answers from the returns handbook: it searches the handbook, pastes the closest passages into the prompt, and answers from them. A customer was told sealed headphones could come back after 20 days. The handbook says electronics get 15.
problem.task: Find out what the model was handed, and why.

bench.heading: The model only reads what you pull from the case.
bench.body: An embedder turns each chunk of the handbook, and the question, into a vector. The closest chunks, by cosine similarity, go into the prompt. Change how the handbook is cut and how many chunks are pulled, and watch the ranking and the answer.
bench.observe: Cut every 160 characters and ask about the headphones. Read which chunks were pulled, and what's missing from them.

measure.heading: Cut, pull, ask.
measure.body: Predict first, then ask all three questions with each cut, two chunks each. A judge reads every answer against the handbook's answer key.

debrief.heading: Retrieval decides what the model can know.

points.one: The model answers from the chunks it's handed. If the rule isn't in them, the answer can't follow it, however good the model is.
points.two: Cutting by size splits rules from what they apply to: 'They have a shorter window' means nothing without the sentence before it. Cut along the document's own structure.
points.three: Embeddings rank by closeness, not by truth. Look at what was retrieved before you blame the model.
points.four: With nothing retrieved, the best answer is 'I don't know'. Ask for it in the prompt, and count it separately from wrong answers.

debrief.voice: A compositor can only set the sorts in the stick. Fill it with the wrong ones and the line reads wrong.

problem.heading: The night shift paid for one blender twice.
problem.body: Mercadito left its assistant on overnight to work the returns queue alone. In the morning the till was 4,900 MXN short for a 2,450 MXN blender. The customer had written twice; each ticket looked new.
problem.task: Run the night yourself, then build a harness that wouldn't have paid twice.

bench.heading: The agent is a loop. The harness is everything around it.
bench.body: The agent asks for a tool; the harness decides. Each request passes a gate (your refund rule) on its way to a real MCP server. You choose the parts: a step limit, a person who approves big refunds, notes carried between tickets, a sub-agent that reads records so the agent doesn't have to.
bench.observe: Run the queue with refunds allowed. Then switch one part at a time and read where the run changes.

measure.heading: Make the till balance.
measure.body: Predict what tonight costs as it stands, then change the harness until the blender is paid for exactly once.

debrief.heading: The model proposes. The harness disposes.

points.one: An agent is a model calling tools in a loop. MCP plugs the tools in; it doesn't decide what's allowed. That happens outside the model: at the gate, at the step limit, and with the people the harness asks.
points.two: The agent knows only its context. Without notes carried between tickets, a repeat ticket looks new, and it pays again.
points.three: A person in the loop is only as good as what the person sees. Approve twice without the notes and the till is just as short.
points.four: A sub-agent keeps raw records out of the agent's context, at the price of extra calls and a summary that can drop the detail you needed.

debrief.voice: A press runs as fast as it's fed. Someone still has to count the sheets.

problem.heading: Before it could set a line, it had to learn the alphabet.
problem.body: Every model in this course started as random numbers. Training nudges those numbers, a step at a time, to make the next character more likely. Here you cast a tiny one from nothing, on a page of proverbs.
problem.task: Watch noise turn into style, and then into something worse.

bench.heading: Loss goes down. Watch what else happens.
bench.body: The model trains on most of the proverbs and never sees the rest. Training loss measures the lines it learns from; held-out loss measures the lines it never sees. Samples show what it has learned, three lines at a time.
bench.observe: Find the step where the two curves part. Read the samples on each side of it.

measure.heading: Count the copies.
measure.body: Predict first, then cast the full run and count how many sampled lines are training lines copied whole.

debrief.heading: Training lowers loss on what it sees. That's all it does.

points.one: Training is next-token prediction plus a nudge: compare the predicted character with the real one, and move every weight a little to make the real one likelier.
points.two: Style comes before content. Early samples have the shape of a proverb (capital, short clauses, a full stop) and none of the words.
points.three: Held-out loss is the honest number. When it turns up while training loss keeps falling, the model is memorizing, not learning.
points.four: Big models face the same trade-off with far more data. Memorized training text is why models can quote their sources word for word.

debrief.voice: A new caster makes bad type for a while. Then, if no one stops it, it makes the same good letter forever.

problem.heading: Retraining every weight costs a foundry. Mercadito has a desk.
problem.body: Fine-tuning a 2B model in full needs about 40 GB just for weights and optimizer. Mercadito's machine has one 12 GB card. LoRA trains a thin plate laid over the weights instead, and leaves the casting alone.
problem.task: Count what the plate costs on a real model, then lay one on a small model and see what it changes.

bench.heading: Freeze the casting. Train the plate.
bench.body: Above, the arithmetic on MiniCPM5-2B's real shapes. Below, an adapter trained live on chapter 11's model: proverbs in, taglines out, with the base weights fingerprinted before and after.
bench.observe: Switch the adapter off and on. Same base weights, different output.

measure.heading: How thin can the plate be?
measure.body: Predict first, then train all three ranks and count the lines that carry a price.

debrief.heading: A small plate changes behaviour, not the casting.

points.one: LoRA adds B·A to chosen weight matrices. With rank 16 on attention, that's about 0.3% of MiniCPM5-2B's parameters.
points.two: The base never changes. One base can carry many adapters, swapped in per task, and switching one off restores the original exactly.
points.three: QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4 bits, which is how a 2B or even a 7B model fine-tunes on a single home GPU.
points.four: Here the plate moved the format (prices, 'Free shipping') more than the words. That's the pattern you'll see again: adapters teach behaviour more readily than facts.

debrief.voice: You don't recast the type to print a new job. You lock a new forme around it.

stages.title: The stages of a real model

problem.heading: One model, four castings.
problem.body: A model you chat with is the last of several training runs. MiniCPM5-2B publishes four of them: the base model, a mid-training checkpoint, the supervised fine-tune and the release. Same architecture, same size, different training.
problem.task: Read what each stage writes for the same prompt, and tell them apart before you're told.

bench.heading: Sort the answers by stage.
bench.body: Each prompt was sent, byte for byte, to all four checkpoints. The answers come back shuffled. Mark which stage wrote each one, then reveal.
bench.observe: Look for what changes from stage to stage: format, length, refusals, language, and mistakes that appear late.

measure.heading: Check the answers.
measure.body: Predict which stage passes the most checks, then read the table.

debrief.heading: Each stage changes behaviour, and each can break something.

points.one: Pretraining makes a model that predicts text. Today's pretraining data is full of questions and answers, so even this base model already answers like an assistant.
points.two: Supervised fine-tuning teaches the format of a good answer from worked examples. RL then rewards outcomes: right answers on math and code, preferred replies elsewhere.
points.three: Later isn't better at everything. Here the release answers a plain fact wrongly in Spanish, and several stages loop on a Spanish proverb.
points.four: This is one small model, greedy, at one setting. Treat it as a look inside the pipeline, not a benchmark.

debrief.voice: Every pass through the press adds a colour. Sometimes it covers one you wanted.

problem.heading: The model will learn every row, the bad ones too.
problem.body: Mercadito wants its support model to write in the house style. Before any training, someone collected sixty replies from the help desk's history. Some are fine. Some aren't.
problem.task: Clean the set before it goes to the press.

bench.heading: Read every row. Mark what you'd remove.
bench.body: A fine-tune copies what it's shown: the style, the policy, and every mistake. Look for duplicates, replies that contradict the policy sheet, answers no customer should get, and rows that also sit in your eval sets.
bench.observe: Mark at least one row, then move on to measure.

measure.heading: Then let the checks read it.
measure.body: Predict what the mechanical checks will catch, run them, then run the judge, and compare all three with what was planted.

debrief.heading: Checks find copies. People and judges find mistakes.

points.one: Duplicates over-weight whatever they repeat. Exact ones are easy to find; reworded ones need fuzzier matching.
points.two: A row that also appears in your eval set makes the eval a memory test. Check every training row against every eval case before you train.
points.three: A contradiction in the data becomes a contradiction in the model. Text matching can't see it; a judge with the policy can, and it also raises false alarms.
points.four: A model judge is a reviewer's first pass, not the last word. Read what it flags before you delete or keep.

debrief.voice: A forme set with one wrong sort prints the wrong sort a thousand times.

problem.heading: "Let's train it" can mean seven different jobs.
problem.body: Mercadito's team keeps saying the model should be trained: on the catalog, on the tone, on the policy, to be cheaper. Each of those is a different kind of training, with different data, a different cost and a different failure.
problem.task: Learn what each kind needs and what it can't do.

bench.heading: The ledger.
bench.body: Seven methods, the data each needs, and what each changes. The last column is hidden. Guess what each one can't do before you open it.
bench.observe: Then read MiniCPM5's own pipeline, from chapter 12, as a row of these methods.

measure.heading: Match the jobs.
measure.body: Pick a method for each job, then check against the ledger.

debrief.heading: Pick the method by the data you have and the change you need.

points.one: Pretraining and continued pretraining take raw text and change what the model knows. They don't teach it to follow your format.
points.two: SFT imitates examples: the fastest way to a format or a tone, and no better than the examples.
points.three: Preference methods (RLHF, DPO) and RL with checkers push the model toward answers someone or something prefers. Each optimises its signal, flaws included.
points.four: Distillation makes a cheaper copy of a stronger model, mistakes included. The field moves fast here: treat the boundaries in this ledger as today's, not permanent.

debrief.voice: A shop has a tool for each job. Using the wrong one still leaves a mark.

problem.heading: Fine-tuning is the most expensive answer to most questions.
problem.body: Every week someone at Mercadito proposes training a model. Most of the time a better prompt or retrieval would do, sooner and cheaper. Sometimes fine-tuning really is the answer.
problem.task: Look at what a real fine-tune learned, then make six calls.

bench.heading: Behaviour sticks. Facts don't.
bench.body: A small fine-tune on forty rows: the sign-off appeared everywhere; the facts in those rows barely moved. Read the example answer.
bench.observe: Ask yourself which of Mercadito's problems are behaviour and which are facts.

measure.heading: Make the calls.
measure.body: Pick an approach for each case, then check.

debrief.heading: Train behaviour. Retrieve facts. Prompt first.

points.one: Fine-tuning teaches format, tone and task behaviour far more reliably than facts. A fact seen in training is recalled in its training wording, not on demand.
points.two: Facts that change, or must be quoted exactly, belong in retrieval, where you can update them and show the source.
points.three: Prompt first, with an eval. Fine-tune when a measured prompt has stopped improving and the behaviour still matters.
points.four: Distill when a big model already solves a narrow task and the volume makes it too expensive.

debrief.voice: You don't cast new type for one poster. You set it from the case.

problem.heading: The fine-tune worked. What did it break?
problem.body: Chapter 16's fine-tune learned Mercadito's sign-off. Before it ships, run the same evals on the model before and after training, including questions it was never meant to change.
problem.task: Use the eval runner from Act II on both models, and find what got worse.

bench.heading: Same evals, two models.
bench.body: Two sets: the support replies the training was for, and general questions it wasn't. Every case, every grader, before and after.
bench.observe: Read the general questions closely. A model that sounds the same can know less.

measure.heading: Count the regressions.
measure.body: Predict how many general checks fail after training, then read each one.

debrief.heading: Evaluate what you didn't train for.

points.one: A fine-tune changes more than its target. Here it learned the sign-off and lost facts it had before.
points.two: Keep an eval of general skills next to the task eval, and run both on every candidate, before and after.
points.three: Small data and many passes over it (here about ten over forty rows) make regressions likelier. Fewer steps, more varied rows or a lower rank are the first knobs to turn.
points.four: If a regression matters more than the gain, don't ship. A prompt or retrieval may get most of the gain without the loss.

debrief.voice: Proof every forme after you change it, not just the line you touched.

problem.heading: Mercadito wants AI in four places by next month.
problem.body: The commission: order status, gift search, return eligibility and product descriptions, all 'with AI'. Some of these are a database lookup. One is a table of rules. One really is fuzzy.
problem.task: Pick rules, search or an LLM for each, and run the month.

bench.heading: Choose a tool for each job, then count what it cost.
bench.body: Each option has a coverage (the rest goes to a person), an accuracy, a cost per wrong answer and a latency. Where the course measured a number earlier, it says which chapter; the rest are assumptions on the page.
bench.observe: Run the month with an LLM everywhere. Then read which line of the bill is biggest.

measure.heading: Find the cheapest month.
measure.body: Predict how many features need an LLM, then try plans until you beat your first one.

debrief.heading: Use an LLM where the input is fuzzy and a mistake is cheap.

points.one: If the answer is a lookup or a table, code is cheaper, faster and right every time it applies. Send the rest to a person.
points.two: The API bill is usually the smallest line. Wrong answers and the people who fix them are the real cost.
points.three: An LLM earns its place where requests are open-ended ("a gift for my dad") and a wrong answer costs little.
points.four: Change an assumption and the answer changes. Write yours down before the meeting, not after.

debrief.voice: Not every job needs the big press. Some need a rubber stamp.

design-for-failure.title: Designing for failure
design-for-failure.kicker: Streaming, uncertainty, undo, the last word

problem.heading: The model will be wrong. The question is who finds out.
problem.body: Chapter 9's assistant was right two times in three, confidently wrong once in nine, and unsure the rest. Mercadito is putting it in front of customers anyway.
problem.task: Design the interface around the mistakes, and count the harm that still gets through.

bench.heading: Five safeguards. Try them alone and together.
bench.body: Each safeguard changes what happens after the model answers. The preview shows the same wrong answer under your design. Every number behind the simulation is on the page.
bench.observe: Turn on streaming alone and run it. Read the harm column.

measure.heading: Which one matters most?
measure.body: Predict, then see each safeguard alone against none.

debrief.heading: Design for the wrong answer, not the right one.

points.one: An honest "I don't know" turns guesses into hand-offs. It costs people's time and saves customers from wrong answers.
points.two: Before an action, put a confirmation or an undo between the model and the money. Show what will happen in plain words.
points.three: Faster isn't safer. Streaming keeps people waiting, which also means more of them read, and act on, the wrong answers.
points.four: Visible uncertainty only helps if the model's uncertainty tracks its errors, and if people read it. Measure both.

debrief.voice: Every proof has errors. The shop that catches them before the run keeps its customers.

problem.heading: The first invoice was three times the estimate.
problem.body: The returns assistant runs on the strong model for every ticket, and every turn re-sends the whole prompt. Finance wants it under $1,000 a month without making the hard tickets worse.
problem.task: Find where the money goes, then cut it.

bench.heading: Every token, every turn, every day.
bench.body: Change the traffic, the prompt sizes, the routing and the cache, and watch each line of the bill. Prices come from the dated table; the cache hit rate and the reply times are assumptions you can see.
bench.observe: Shrink the system prompt by half. Then turn on caching instead. Compare.

measure.heading: Get under budget.
measure.body: Predict the bill as it stands, then bring it under $1,000 a month with the hard tickets still on the strong model.

debrief.heading: Input is the bill. Route it, and cache what repeats.

points.one: A conversation re-sends the system prompt and its history on every turn, so input tokens usually outweigh output.
points.two: Route by difficulty: a cheap model for the easy majority, the strong one where it measurably matters.
points.three: Cache the stable prefix. Reads cost a tenth of input on Haiku 5.5 and a twentieth on Sonnet 5.5; writes cost a quarter more. It needs steady traffic inside the cache window.
points.four: Prices change and routing changes quality. Re-check both against the price page and your evals before you trust a saving.

debrief.voice: Paper is cheap. Setting the same page twice is not.

problem.heading: Launch day is the easy part.
problem.body: The returns assistant goes live the week before the November sale. Nothing breaks on day one. The bills, the invented policies and the first attack arrive later.
problem.task: Write a launch plan, then live through eight weeks of it.

bench.heading: Plan, defend, launch, wait.
bench.body: Switch on the parts of your plan, set your defenses in the lab, and launch. Each week shows what happened; mistakes are paid for the week after. Every number lives in the chapter's content, and earlier chapters supplied the costs.
bench.observe: Launch with nothing switched on. Watch week 3, then week 5.

measure.heading: Make it survive.
measure.body: Predict the cost of launching as it stands, then find a plan that stays under budget and stops every harmful injection.

debrief.heading: Plan for the bill, the mistakes and the attacker before launch day.

points.one: Traffic isn't flat. A sale triples it, and a per-conversation cost triples with it unless something caps the spend.
points.two: Mistakes cost more than tokens, and they arrive late. Ground the answers that commit money, and check them before they reach a customer.
points.three: Telling the model to ignore injected instructions only weakens an attack. What stops it is architecture: gates on actions, agents without tools for untrusted text, filters on what leaves.
points.four: Untrusted text, private data and a way to send things out, together in one agent, is the dangerous combination. Break at least one link.

debrief.voice: A press runs fine on the first sheet. It's the ten-thousandth that finds the flaw.

finale.title: The commission
finale.kicker: Finale: design a feature, face the board

problem.heading: Mercadito's last commission is yours to design.
problem.body: Customers write every day to ask where a late order is. Mercadito wants an assistant that answers from the order record, apologizes properly, and may offer a small coupon when it's really late. You've done every piece of this in the course.
problem.task: Write the spec, the prompt, the evals, the guardrails and the launch plan. Then face the review board.

bench.heading: Five parts, your words.
bench.body: Nothing here is graded while you write. The board reads it only when you submit, and every check it makes is a lesson from an earlier chapter.
bench.observe: Write the goal first. Everything else follows from it.

measure.heading: The review board.
measure.body: Predict how many will approve, submit, and revise until all four do.

debrief.heading: That's the course.

points.one: Inside the model: tokens, probabilities, a window that fills, and fluency that isn't truth.
points.two: The craft: prompts as specs, evals before opinions, schemas, tools, retrieval and a harness around every agent.
points.three: The foundry: training lowers loss on what it sees, fine-tuning teaches behaviour better than facts, and every change needs a regression test.
points.four: The commissions: pick the right tool, design for the wrong answer, read the bill, and launch slowly.

debrief.voice: The type goes back in the case. The job is printed.

why.petrov-2023: Measures how much more some languages pay, across many tokenizers.
why.karpathy-tokenizer: Builds a byte-pair tokenizer from scratch; the clearest intuition for where sorts come from.
why.tiktoken: The tokenizer library behind the o200k_base case used on this bench.
why.anthropic-token-counting: How to get exact Claude token counts before you send a request.
why.holtzman-2019: Where top-p (nucleus sampling) comes from, and why pure greedy text degenerates.
why.karpathy-gpt: Builds a small GPT and shows logits, softmax and sampling in a few hundred lines.
why.vaswani-2017: The transformer paper. Dense, but this is where the compositor's machinery starts.
why.liu-2023: The study behind "lost in the middle": accuracy by position across models and context lengths.
why.anthropic-long-context: Practical advice on placing long documents and questions in a prompt.
why.kalai-2025: Argues models hallucinate because training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty.
why.ji-2023: A broad survey of hallucination: kinds, causes, metrics and mitigations.
why.anthropic-hallucinations: Concrete techniques to reduce made-up answers, including letting the model say it doesn't know.
why.anthropic-prompting: Anthropic's guide to writing clear, specific prompts, with examples.
why.openai-prompting: OpenAI's guide to the same craft; most of the advice transfers between models.
why.husain-evals: Why evals come first, and how to build them from real failures.
why.huyen-ai-engineering: A book-length treatment of building on foundation models, with a long section on evaluation.
why.zheng-2023-judge: Measures how far LLM judges agree with people, and their biases (position, length, self-preference).
why.anthropic-structured-outputs: How to constrain Claude's output to a JSON Schema, and which schema features are supported.
why.zod-json-schema: Converting Zod schemas to JSON Schema, the bridge used on this bench.
why.anthropic-tool-use: How Claude requests tools, and how your code returns results: the loop on this bench, in the native format.
why.openai-function-calling: The same contract on OpenAI's API: function definitions, calls and outputs.
why.lewis-2020-rag: The paper that named retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve passages, then generate from them.
why.wang-2024-me5: The embedder on this bench: how it was trained and why queries and passages get different prefixes.
why.anthropic-contextual-retrieval: Chunks lose their context when cut. One fix: write that context back into each chunk before embedding it.
why.anthropic-building-agents: When to build an agent at all, and the simpler workflows that often do the job instead.
why.mcp-spec: The protocol between the harness and the tools: how tools are listed and called.
why.xstate-docs: The state machine library that runs this harness's loop: states, guards and invoked calls.
why.karpathy-nanogpt: The smallest serious GPT trainer; the model on this bench is a toy version of the same idea.
why.hu-2021-lora: The LoRA paper: freeze the weights, train a low-rank update, merge it or swap it at will.
why.dettmers-2023-qlora: LoRA on a 4-bit base: the memory arithmetic that puts fine-tuning on one consumer GPU.
why.minicpm5-card: The model whose shapes and checkpoints this act uses: its training stages, data and licence.
why.ouyang-2022-instructgpt: The paper that made the pipeline standard: pretrain, supervised fine-tune, then learn from human preferences.
why.lambert-2024-tulu3: A fully documented post-training recipe, including how the training data was mixed, cleaned and decontaminated against evals.
why.rafailov-2023-dpo: Preference tuning without a reward model or RL loop: the method behind many open fine-tunes.
why.hinton-2015-distillation: The original distillation paper: a small model learns from a big one's probabilities.
why.anthropic-prompt-caching: How prompt caching works, what it costs, and how long a cached prefix lives.
why.anthropic-pricing: Current prices per model, including cache writes, cache reads and batch discounts.
why.owasp-llm01: The industry's reference entry on prompt injection: direct and indirect, with mitigations.
why.greshake-2023: The paper that showed indirect prompt injection against real LLM-integrated apps.
why.willison-lethal-trifecta: Why an agent with private data, untrusted content and a way out is exploitable, whatever the prompt says.
